In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how automaticity and attention interact.
the question of how the brain is able to process a large amount of information in a very short period of time and to respond in a timely manner.
the role of attention in automatic processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
automatic processes are modulated by attention.
automatic processes are not automatic in the sense that they can be performed in a completely resource independent manner.
attentional modulation of unconscious automatic processes can be obtained, and that this modulation is mediated by the attentional allocation process, which is itself an automatic process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
attentional modulation of automatic processes is a function of temporal attention to the stimulus, and that temporal attention to stimuli is a prerequisite for the occurrence of automatic processes.
automatic processes are not as independent of cognitive resources as previously assumed.
attention is necessary for the emergence of automatic priming, even in the case of unconscious priming effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
attentional modulation of unconscious automatic processes does occur and that it can be studied with ERPs.
automatic processes are not independent of attention, but can be modulated in the time window in which they occur.
automatic processes are not as automatic as they are often assumed to be.
